title: What an LLM does
subtitle: Spoiler: it guesses the next word (really well)
mission: Make the model continue “Once upon a…” and find out how it writes: all at once or bit by bit?

predict.question: guess before you run! To continue “Once upon a”, how does the model write?

options.onebyone: One word at a time, looking at what it already wrote
options.search: It looks the continuation up on the internet

feedback.right: yes! It picked one word out of a few candidates. To write more, it appends that word and picks the next one looking at everything again.
feedback.wrong: close! Look at the scene: it picked just one word, out of a few candidates. To write more, it repeats the process, one word at a time.
feedback.skipped: skipped the guess, huh? That’s fine: notice it picked just one word, out of a few candidates.

coach.ui: guess noted. Keep “Once upon a” and hit Run.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run the command below (Enter or Run).

why.simples:
It’s like your phone’s autocomplete, only trained far more. It has read so much text that it learned which words tend to follow which.
To write a sentence, it makes a guess, appends it, and makes another guess looking at everything again. Word by word.
why.dev:
An LLM is a function that takes a sequence of tokens and returns a probability distribution over the next token. Generation is autoregressive: pick a token, append it to the input, run the model again.
This simulator only looks at the last word (a bigram model). A real LLM uses the whole context, with attention (transformer), which is why it doesn’t lose track.
why.especialista:
Each generated token is a pass through the network (with a KV cache so the past isn’t recomputed): latency grows with output length, and cost is billed per input and output token.
“Just predicting the next token” undersells what emerges: to predict well, the model has to represent facts, grammar and reasoning. It also explains the limit: it optimizes plausibility, not truth. That comes back in step 8.

formula: P(next | text so far) → pick → append → repeat

mission.ui: time to break it. Tap the “Flibber” example (or type a made-up word) and run.
mission.cmd: time to break it. Run predict "Flibber" --words 5 (or any made-up word).

break.success: Broken: the model never saw “{word}”, so it guessed common words with almost equal chances. It doesn’t “know” anything beyond what it learned; it just follows patterns.
break.calm: It knew that one. Try a word that never existed.

ui: Leave the text as it is and hit Run.
To see more than one word, drag “Words”.
To break it: tap the “Flibber” example and run.
cmd: The text goes in quotes, right after predict.
--words says how many words it writes.

errors.aboveMax.steps: Up to 12 words at a time: this toy model has a tiny vocabulary and would start repeating itself.
errors.belowMin.steps: Zero words? Then the model doesn’t even wake up. Use 1 to 12.
errors.notInteger.steps: There are no half words here: use a whole number, like 4.
